event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency after rapid snowmelt flooding and Winter Storm Wesley
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The snow took longer to melt on the Minnesota side of the northern Red River Valley, than it did in the southern Red River Valley. At the National Weather Service office in Grand Forks, the snow depth fell to zero on April 6th. However, a blizzard from April 10th to 12th brought more snow to the area. This snow finally melted by April 15th. As the snow melted, it flooded low lying areas and roads. Some sections of land pooled with water from the snow melt, but more so closer to the Red River. In the city of East Grand Forks, the point bridge and the Sorlie bridge were closed due to high water in the Red River.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency after rapid snowmelt flooding and Winter Storm Wesley
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: There were multiple waves of precipitation that occurred with this major winter storm that lasted for more than two days. ||The first wave of precipitation developed during the morning of Wednesday, April 10th where the initial band moved from southern Minnesota, northward into central Minnesota, and west central Wisconsin by the afternoon and evening. This band of precipitation had thunder, sleet and heavy snow that produced several inches of snow across portions of southern and central Minnesota. Most of the heavier precipitation tapered off in the southern quarter of Minnesota, with light snow continuing across central Minnesota, during the afternoon and evening of Thursday, April 11th.  ||The second wave of precipitation developed in far southern Minnesota after midnight, Thursday morning, April 11th. This band of precipitation had warmer air aloft which led to more sleet, rain, freezing rain, and thunder. This band was similar to the first with the intensity, but had more mixed precipitation.||By the mid morning, the wave of precipitation had moved out of the region, with much warmer air surging northward ahead of a surface low that moved into southwest Minnesota during the afternoon. There were even some severe thunderstorms that developed near Redwood Falls where one inch hail was reported.||In addition to the precipitation Thursday morning, the next weather element developed. This weather element was a significant increase in the wind speeds, with sustained winds of 30 to 40 mph, with gusts of 50 mph or more across a wide areas of central, and southern Minnesota. This created blizzard conditions in portions of southwest, and west central Minnesota. It would have been worse if the precipitation was in the form of all snow, but warmer air aloft led to more sleet and rain, vs snow. ||The high winds also created structural damage to power poles and trees. Some freezing rain led to fallen tree limbs and power outages from ice build up. The local emergency manager in Freeborn County had more than 300 downed power poles, which affected 6500 residents. The Waseca County emergency manager also reported numerous power poles blown down across the county. The National Guard was requested for Freeborn and Steele Counties of south central Minnesota due to stranded motorists. The Governor of Minnesota declared a state of emergency due to the widespread power outages, and stranded motorists. ||By Thursday afternoon, most of the heavier precipitation and thunderstorms had moved north and east of the area, with mainly light precipitation in the form of drizzle, light snow or sleet in small areas rotating northward as the main storm started to weaken and move overhead.  In addition, wind speeds lessened which led to much better visibility in the west. However, the Minnesota Department of Transportation had already closed or not advised travel for a wide area of west central to southwest Minnesota. ||The third wave of precipitation was associated with the main upper level system and changed the precipitation over to all snow by early Friday morning, April 12th. By the afternoon, most of the precipitation had ended, but residual light snow or flurries continued as the main system moved off to the east.||Snowfall totals as the storm ended ranged from over 18 inches in portions of west central Minnesota, to 6 to 12 inches across a wide area of central and southern Minnesota. Areas along the Iowa border, which had more sleet and rain, received 1 to locally 4 inches of snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several waves of precipitation occurred across the county with heavy snow at the start, with a mixture of sleet, and snow during the overnight hours before transitioning to mainly light snow, drizzle Wednesday evening, and Thursday. Snowfall totals averaged 7 to 9 inches across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historic blizzard affected west central Minnesota from April 11th to the 12th. The storm came in two waves. The first wave brought a band of moderate to heavy snow as it lifted from south to north across the region during the morning hours of the 10th. The second wave of heavy snow and strong north winds were with the main surface low pressure area moving across the central plains. The heavy snow in combination with winds gusting to over 40 mph brought blizzard conditions along with heavy drifting. At the storm's end, locations reported very heavy snowfall amounts of 13 to 18 inches. ||The blizzard impacted cattle producers, roads, schools, businesses, and more. This storm also exacerbated the ongoing flooding with the addition of more snowmelt water. Some snowfall amounts include 13 inches at Wheaton and Browns Valley and 18 inches at Artichoke Lake and Ortonville.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency after rapid snowmelt flooding and Winter Storm Wesley
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed in the lee of the Rockies late on the 10th and then slowly moved northeast on the 11th before passing over the Northland on the 12th. This lead to a long duration snowfall event over most of the area with periods of freezing rain mixing in at times. Widespread strong northeast winds of 40 mph plus were reported with upwards of 50 to 60 mph gusts observed at the head of Lake Superior. The strong winds lead to building waves on Lake Superior, but the ice that was still present at the western end of the lake acted to dampen the wave action, preventing the large waves from crashing onto the lakeshore. The winds also led to numerous reports of downed trees and power lines with multiple vehicle crashes due to the snow and freezing rain. Snowfall amounts were generally in the 3 to 9 inch range with the highest totals being 10.9 inches in Chisholm, 11.0 inches just north of Knife River and 13.5 inches near Pine River.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency after rapid snowmelt flooding and Winter Storm Wesley
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong early April Colorado Low took shape over the Central Plains late Wednesday afternoon, April 10th. The surface low tracked nearly straight northward on Thursday, April 11th, reaching the Sioux Falls, South Dakota, area late in the afternoon. As it lifted northward, bands of heavy snow spread into southeast North Dakota and west central Minnesota. Some of these bands of snow produced snow rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour. Generally most of this area received 6 to 12 inches of snow, but the Havana, North Dakota, and Bemidji, Minnesota, areas received 14 to 18 inches.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency after rapid snowmelt flooding and Winter Storm Wesley
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From Thursday night into Friday, April 12th, the low finally turned northeast and tracked toward Duluth. Wind speeds were not intensely strong during this blizzard event, as most sites only gusted into the 40 to 45 mph range. This event did occur during the spring snowmelt flood, when many rivers and ditches were filled with water. This brought an additional threat of vehicles sliding off slippery roads into water filled ditches. Interstate 29 was closed in eastern North Dakota and Interstate 94 was closed from Jamestown, North Dakota, to Osakis, Minnesota. Many other roads were either closed or had travel not recommended.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency after rapid snowmelt flooding and Winter Storm Wesley
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historic late-season, multi-day winter storm developed rapidly across the central Plains on Wednesday, April 10. This system spiraled several periods of precipitation through the region. The leading precipitation on April 10 was a mix of rain, freezing rain and sleet from far eastern South Dakota through the Interstate 90 areas of southwest Minnesota and northwest Iowa, changing to snow to the north and west. There were even a few elevated thunderstorms which occurred overnight on April 10-11 and produced some near severe hail, which actually occurred after some initial wintry precipitation. Significant icing was centered around 30 miles either side of the Interstate 90 corridor, with as much as a third to three-quarters inch ice accumulation. ||Heavy snowfall developed from the early morning of April 11 and continued into the early morning of April 12 across much of southeast South Dakota into northern portions of southwest Minnesota, which accumulated to 1 to 2 feet during the storm. The most persistent snowfall occurred for areas west to north of Sioux Falls, but even there, a brief period of freezing rain or sleet occurred at some point ahead of the main upper trough passage. ||The other aspect of this storm was the intense winds, which gusted at the peak from 40 to 60 mph, producing widespread blizzard conditions across southeast South Dakota and southwest Minnesota. Considerable power outages occurred as transmission lines succumbed to the ice accumulation and wind.  At the peak, electric companies and cooperatives estimated as many as 25,000 customers were without power.  Many areas were without power for a day or two due to the intensity of the storm. ||In fact, the strong winds lofted dust from the Texas/Oklahoma panhandles which caused some of the snowfall toward the latter portions of the event to fall with a brownish color.  Ironically, the blizzard postponed the statewide tornado warning drill which was a part of Minnesota Severe Weather Awareness Week.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Blizzard conditions led to a shutdown of government offices and schools, and travel was not recommended with many roads closed due to the widespread whiteout conditions. Storm-total snowfall from 4 to 10 inches occurred, with 5.1 inches at Windom. With winds gusting at times from 40 to 50 mph, many areas had snow drifts of several feet, making roads impassable. Ice accumulation from one-quarter to one-half inch occurred, and helped to produce scattered power outages as snowfall and wind increased. Damage costs are rough estimates due to utility costs.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency after rapid snowmelt flooding and Winter Storm Wesley
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong early spring storm system produced snow, sleet and freezing rain across southeast Minnesota from April 10th into the 11th. Snowfall amounts generally ranged from 3 to 7 inches. Strong east winds brought down power poles and lines where enough freezing rain occurred to coat exposed surfaces. Around 100 power poles were downed across Mower County and the entire town of Rushford (Fillmore County) lost power. The highest reported snowfall total was 11 inches on the northeast side of Rochester (Olmsted County). The highest recorded wind gust was 56 mph by the automated weather observing equipment at the Rochester airport. The Governor of Minnesota declared a state  of emergency and ordered the National Guard to assist as needed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: COOP and volunteer snow observers reported that around 5 inches of snow fell across Dodge County. In addition to the snow, a period of sleet and freezing rain occurred that coated exposed surfaces with a glaze of ice. With the glaze of ice, some power poles and lines were brought down across the southern part of the county by the strong winds causing around 4,000 people to lose power. At least three county roads were closed because of downed power lines. A countywide state of emergency was declared with shelters opened for those without power.

Many areas were without power for a day or two due to the intensity of the storm. ||In fact, the strong winds lofted dust from the Texas/Oklahoma panhandles which caused some of the snowfall toward the latter portions of the event to fall with a brownish color. Many roads were closed, including U.S. Highway 71, State Highway 86, and Interstate 90 due to power structures across roadways. Damage costs are rough estimates due to utility costs.

The leading precipitation on April 10 was a mix of rain, freezing rain and sleet from far eastern South Dakota through the Interstate 90 areas of southwest Minnesota and northwest Iowa, changing to snow to the north and west. There were even a few elevated thunderstorms which occurred overnight on April 10-11 and produced some near severe hail, which actually occurred after some initial wintry precipitation. Significant icing was centered around 30 miles either side of the Interstate 90 corridor, with as much as a third to three-quarters inch ice accumulation. ||Heavy snowfall developed from the early morning of April 11 and continued into the early morning of April 12 across much of southeast South Dakota into northern portions of southwest Minnesota, which accumulated to 1 to 2 feet during the storm. The most persistent snowfall occurred for areas west to north of Sioux Falls, but even there, a brief period of freezing rain or sleet occurred at some point ahead of the main upper trough passage. ||The other aspect of this storm was the intense winds, which gusted at the peak from 40 to 60 mph, producing widespread blizzard conditions across southeast South Dakota and southwest Minnesota. Considerable power outages occurred as transmission lines succumbed to the ice accumulation and wind.  At the peak, electric companies and cooperatives estimated as many as 25,000 customers were without power.  Many areas were without power for a day or two due to the intensity of the storm. ||In fact, the strong winds lofted dust from the Texas/Oklahoma panhandles which caused some of the snowfall toward the latter portions of the event to fall with a brownish color.  Ironically, the blizzard postponed the statewide tornado warning drill which was a part of Minnesota Severe Weather Awareness Week.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Blizzard conditions and ice accumulations led to a shutdown of government offices and schools, and travel was not recommended with many roads closed due to the widespread whiteout conditions. Storm-total snowfall from 4 to 10 inches occurred, with 6.0 inches near Edgerton and 5.5 inches at Pipestone. With winds gusting at times from 45 to 55 mph, many areas had snow drifts of several feet, making roads impassable. Ice accumulation from a tenth to a third of an inch occurred, and helped to produce scattered power outages as wind increased. Damage costs are rough estimates due to utility costs.

The surface low tracked nearly straight northward on Thursday, April 11th, reaching the Sioux Falls, South Dakota, area late in the afternoon. As it lifted northward, bands of heavy snow spread into southeast North Dakota and west central Minnesota. Some of these bands of snow produced snow rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour. Generally most of this area received 6 to 12 inches of snow, but the Havana, North Dakota, and Bemidji, Minnesota, areas received 14 to 18 inches.

This lead to a long duration snowfall event over most of the area with periods of freezing rain mixing in at times. Widespread strong northeast winds of 40 mph plus were reported with upwards of 50 to 60 mph gusts observed at the head of Lake Superior. The strong winds lead to building waves on Lake Superior, but the ice that was still present at the western end of the lake acted to dampen the wave action, preventing the large waves from crashing onto the lakeshore. The winds also led to numerous reports of downed trees and power lines with multiple vehicle crashes due to the snow and freezing rain. Snowfall amounts were generally in the 3 to 9 inch range with the highest totals being 10.9 inches in Chisholm, 11.0 inches just north of Knife River and 13.5 inches near Pine River.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency after rapid snowmelt flooding and Winter Storm Wesley
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: There were multiple waves of precipitation that occurred with this major winter storm that lasted for more than two days. ||The first wave of precipitation developed during the morning of Wednesday, April 10th where the initial band moved from southern Minnesota, northward into central Minnesota, and west central Wisconsin by the afternoon and evening. This band of precipitation had thunder, sleet and heavy snow that produced several inches of snow across portions of southern and central Minnesota. Most of the heavier precipitation tapered off in the southern quarter of Minnesota, with light snow continuing across central Minnesota, during the afternoon and evening of Thursday, April 11th.  ||The second wave of precipitation developed in far southern Minnesota after midnight, Thursday morning, April 11th. This band of precipitation had warmer air aloft which led to more sleet, rain, freezing rain, and thunder. This band was similar to the first with the intensity, but had more mixed precipitation.||By the mid morning, the wave of precipitation had moved out of the region, with much warmer air surging northward ahead of a surface low that moved into southwest Minnesota during the afternoon. There were even some severe thunderstorms that developed near Redwood Falls where one inch hail was reported.||In addition to the precipitation Thursday morning, the next weather element developed. This weather element was a significant increase in the wind speeds, with sustained winds of 30 to 40 mph, with gusts of 50 mph or more across a wide areas of central, and southern Minnesota. This created blizzard conditions in portions of southwest, and west central Minnesota. It would have been worse if the precipitation was in the form of all snow, but warmer air aloft led to more sleet and rain, vs snow. ||The high winds also created structural damage to power poles and trees. Some freezing rain led to fallen tree limbs and power outages from ice build up. The local emergency manager in Freeborn County had more than 300 downed power poles, which affected 6500 residents. The Waseca County emergency manager also reported numerous power poles blown down across the county. The National Guard was requested for Freeborn and Steele Counties of south central Minnesota due to stranded motorists. The Governor of Minnesota declared a state of emergency due to the widespread power outages, and stranded motorists. ||By Thursday afternoon, most of the heavier precipitation and thunderstorms had moved north and east of the area, with mainly light precipitation in the form of drizzle, light snow or sleet in small areas rotating northward as the main storm started to weaken and move overhead.  In addition, wind speeds lessened which led to much better visibility in the west. However, the Minnesota Department of Transportation had already closed or not advised travel for a wide area of west central to southwest Minnesota. ||The third wave of precipitation was associated with the main upper level system and changed the precipitation over to all snow by early Friday morning, April 12th. By the afternoon, most of the precipitation had ended, but residual light snow or flurries continued as the main system moved off to the east.||Snowfall totals as the storm ended ranged from over 18 inches in portions of west central Minnesota, to 6 to 12 inches across a wide area of central and southern Minnesota. Areas along the Iowa border, which had more sleet and rain, received 1 to locally 4 inches of snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several waves of precipitation occurred across the county with heavy snow at the start, with a mixture of sleet, and snow during the overnight hours of Wednesday/Thursday, before mostly light snow and sleet occurred Thursday, and Thursday night. Wind speeds increased Thursday morning, with significant blowing and drifting snow, causing blizzard conditions for several hours. Wind speeds lessened late Thursday afternoon but light snow redeveloped. Snowfall totals averaged 8 to 10 inches across the county.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency after rapid snowmelt flooding and Winter Storm Wesley
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historic blizzard affected west central Minnesota from April 11th to the 12th. The storm came in two waves. The first wave brought a band of moderate to heavy snow as it lifted from south to north across the region during the morning hours of the 10th. The second wave of heavy snow and strong north winds were with the main surface low pressure area moving across the central plains. The heavy snow in combination with winds gusting to over 40 mph brought blizzard conditions along with heavy drifting. At the storm's end, locations reported very heavy snowfall amounts of 13 to 18 inches. ||The blizzard impacted cattle producers, roads, schools, businesses, and more. This storm also exacerbated the ongoing flooding with the addition of more snowmelt water. Some snowfall amounts include 13 inches at Wheaton and Browns Valley and 18 inches at Artichoke Lake and Ortonville.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency after rapid snowmelt flooding and Winter Storm Wesley
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong early spring storm system produced snow, sleet and freezing rain across southeast Minnesota from April 10th into the 11th. Snowfall amounts generally ranged from 3 to 7 inches. Strong east winds brought down power poles and lines where enough freezing rain occurred to coat exposed surfaces. Around 100 power poles were downed across Mower County and the entire town of Rushford (Fillmore County) lost power. The highest reported snowfall total was 11 inches on the northeast side of Rochester (Olmsted County). The highest recorded wind gust was 56 mph by the automated weather observing equipment at the Rochester airport. The Governor of Minnesota declared a state  of emergency and ordered the National Guard to assist as needed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: COOP and volunteer snow observers reported that 6 to 9 inches of snow fell across Wabasha County. In addition to the snow, a period of sleet and freezing rain occurred that coated exposed surfaces with a glaze of ice. The highest reported snowfall total was 9.3 inches near Zumbro Falls.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency after rapid snowmelt flooding and Winter Storm Wesley
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong early April Colorado Low took shape over the Central Plains late Wednesday afternoon, April 10th. The surface low tracked nearly straight northward on Thursday, April 11th, reaching the Sioux Falls, South Dakota, area late in the afternoon. As it lifted northward, bands of heavy snow spread into southeast North Dakota and west central Minnesota. Some of these bands of snow produced snow rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour. Generally most of this area received 6 to 12 inches of snow, but the Havana, North Dakota, and Bemidji, Minnesota, areas received 14 to 18 inches.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing Assistance to Stranded Motorists after a powerful winter storm

Warm air advection caused temperatures across most of east-central Minnesota to rise above freezing and produce mixed precipitation for several hours during the day. As the cold front gradually moved east, temperatures very quickly dropped and caused treacherous road conditions as mixed precipitation changed over to snow. Narrow bands of heavy snow set up over the Brainerd Lakes northeast towards the Iron Range during the early morning and early afternoon, and then translated east towards the Twin Ports, North Shore, and Interstate 35 corridor. The heavy snow bands coincided with the strong mid-level frontogenesis, which also produced very strong northwest winds that caused the widespread blizzard conditions. A maximum gust of 70 mph was recorded at the Bay of Grand Marais during the height of the storm. Although winds gusted up to 60 mph, the lowest visibilities were mainly tied to falling snow. The main snow band moved into the Devils Lake ND region around midnight, shifted into the northern and central Red River Valley around 3 am, then finally into west central Minnesota and the southern Red River Valley around 6 am, with blizzard conditions developing thereafter. The 60 mph winds and falling snow combined to produce whiteout conditions at times, especially in open country. Once the snow ended, the wind did continue to loft the snow particles and keep visibilities low.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: From 1 to 4 inches of fresh snow and winds gusting from 45 to 55 mph combined to produce widespread blizzard conditions.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing Assistance to Stranded Motorists after a powerful winter storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure brought heavy snowfall and very strong winds to much of the Northland starting on Wednesday the 23rd and lingering into Thursday the 24th. This storm was unique in that widespread blizzard conditions occurred across the upper Midwest, including areas from the Brainerd Lakes east towards the North Shore, Twin Ports, and Interstate 35 corridor with many observed wind gusts between 50 and 70 mph. Very strong frontogenesis occurred along a trowal axis that extended across much of northern Wisconsin west into Minnesota. Warm air advection caused temperatures across most of east-central Minnesota to rise above freezing and produce mixed precipitation for several hours during the day. As the cold front gradually moved east, temperatures very quickly dropped and caused treacherous road conditions as mixed precipitation changed over to snow. Narrow bands of heavy snow set up over the Brainerd Lakes northeast towards the Iron Range during the early morning and early afternoon, and then translated east towards the Twin Ports, North Shore, and Interstate 35 corridor. The heavy snow bands coincided with the strong mid-level frontogenesis, which also produced very strong northwest winds that caused the widespread blizzard conditions. A maximum gust of 70 mph was recorded at the Bay of Grand Marais during the height of the storm. Damage was reported to buildings and other infrastructure, in addition to some power outages and widespread whiteout conditions that made travel difficult if not impossible.||As the cold front swept rapidly eastward, bitterly cold air moved into the region and led to the development of a topographically-forced gravity wave during the night of the 23rd that dropped several more inches of snow from Two Harbors to Superior to Holyoke. The eastern half of northeast Minnesota received 6 to 10 inches of snowfall with lesser amounts further west in addition to the widespread blizzard conditions.

Initially, large hail was the primary concern, with an increasingly tornadic environment heading into April 23rd. Both hail (up to 1.5 inches) and tornadoes were reported with this system.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Portions of County Road 92, between Plummer and Red Lake Falls were closed off due to debris jams and flooding along the Clearwater River. The Clearwater River at Plummer rose over 6 feet by the evening of the 23rd, due to the combination of a rapid snowmelt and from 1 to 2 inches of rainfall in the river basin.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing National Guard Assistance to Local Emergency Flood Operations in Minnesota
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of storms moved across southeast Minnesota on May 19th. The first occurred from late morning through the middle of the afternoon and produced primarily large hail across Mower and Olmsted Counties. The largest reported hail with this activity was ping pong ball sized near Lyle (Mower County), Adams (Mower County), south of Rochester (Olmsted County) and east of Rochester. The second round of storms also produced hail, although not as large as the earlier storms. The largest reported hail in the late afternoon was quarter sized north of Genoa (Olmsted County). A large tree, estimated to be four feet in diameter, was blown down near Whalan (Fillmore County). Flash flooding across eastern Winona County caused several mud slides, washouts and some cars were submerged in water. Winona County declared a state of emergency and the Governor of Minnesota authorized emergency assistance to help with the recovery.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Stockton, 3.54 inches of rain fell.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing National Guard Assistance to Stranded Motorists during a winter storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several inches of snow followed by rapid intensification of a low-pressure system over the Great Lakes led to a multi-day winter storm for much of Minnesota. Part 1 of this system was widespread fluffy snow with high snow-to-liquid ratios from southwest through east central Minnesota. There was a break, and then part 2 of this system followed as strong arctic winds developed in wrap-around circulation of the low-pressure system. Wind gusts of 35-50 mph, with the highest speeds in western and southern Minnesota. These winds together with the arctic air and fresh snow led to dangerous wind-chills near -25 to -35��F and blizzard conditions across the open terrain of the Minnesota River Valley. Roads became impassable, and the National Guard was called upon to help rescue folks. Farther north and east it was more wooded, so blizzard conditions didn't develop. Roads were still slick, along with dangerous wind chills.||The highest amounts of observed snowfall appeared to surround eastern MN and western WI. More specifically the Andover and Ham Lake (Andover) in 10.8 inches. Northern Dakota County 8-9 inches near Lakeville and Rosemont. Farther west, Scott County observed 7 to 9 inches in the southeastern part of the county between New Prague and Lakeville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were multiple reports of 8 to 10 inches across the county within a 12-hour period. Highest snowfall observed were near Coon Rapids, MN (9.7 inches) and Ham Lake, MN (10.8 inches). This verifies the winter storm warning.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing National Guard Assistance to Stranded Motorists during a winter storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of Arctic air masses crossed the region over a period of 7 days beginning on Sunday, December 19th. Temperatures failed to even reach 5 degrees above zero during this period through December 26th, with lows consistently dropping into the teens and 20s below zero. An unusually potent blast of cold air for December followed in behind a reinforcing Arctic front Tuesday night, December 20th, into Wednesday, December 21st, along with a trace to as much as 2 to 4 of new snowfall on top of the pre-existing snow pack. Wind gusts of 30 to 50 mph behind this front impacted the region from the 21st through the 23rd, resulting in an extended period of life-threatening wind chills in the -35 to -50 degree F range and near blizzard conditions. The coldest measured wind chills include -48 F at Graceville, -47 F at Wheaton, -45 F at Ortonville (all on the 22nd). ||The extreme cold made the threat to stranded motorists even more dangerous, as numerous roads were deemed No Travel Advised or closed by the Minnesota Department of Transportation. Numerous vehicle accidents occurred, and numerous schools closed throughout the event.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing National Guard Assistance to Stranded Motorists during a winter storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure intensified and moved from the Central Plains into Minnesota. Initially, warm thermal profiles allowed for mixed precipitation or all rain. However, as winds shifted to the northwest, colder air rapidly changed precipitation over to snow. While additional accumulation of snow was fairly light (up to 1 to 3 inches in areas of greatest snowfall along an axis from Tyndall to Salem to Minneota), northwest winds were bolstered to a gusty 40 to 60 mph and resulted in widespread blowing snow along with spotty blizzard conditions near the Buffalo Ridge. Travel was not recommended during the overnight and early morning hours across parts of southwest Minnesota and east central South Dakota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest wind reached gusts to 56 mph at the Minnesota Road Weather Information System site near Jeffers and 53 mph near Mountain Lake, with 48 mph at the Automated Weather Observing System site KMWM near Windom. Despite less than a half inch of new snowfall at Windom, winds whipped up considerable blowing snow with visibility of a half mile or less at times.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing National Guard Assistance to Local Emergency Flood Operations in Minnesota
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On Tuesday, June 18, 2024, a stationary surface front, in conjunction with an anomalously moist airmass over the Northland, resulting in widespread flash flooding. NWS Duluth issued seven Flash Flood Warnings (across much of NE MN and the Bayfield Peninsula), three of which were upgraded to include a considerable tag for life threatening flash flooding. Additionally, severe thunderstorms occurred ahead of the heaviest rainfall, prompting eight Tornado Warnings (near Ely and between Leech Lake and Grand Rapids) and 16 Severe Thunderstorm Warnings. Flash flooding extended from north-central Minnesota to the MN Arrowhead and across Lake Superior to the Bayfield Peninsula. River flooding would continue for weeks after the event, and high water in the Rainy River Basin headwaters would eventually lead to minor flooding after another round of heavy rain in early July. Furthermore, significant tree blowdowns occurred in the Superior National Forest due to damaging wind gusts associated with the storms.||Slow moving heavy rain and thunderstorms tracked across northeastern Minnesota and far northern Wisconsin in the afternoon and evening of Tuesday, June 18, leading to extensive damaging flash flooding that evening, and prolonged areal and river flooding through the end of the week. Scattered rain had been persistent through the day, and then widespread strong storms initiated along a slow moving front with parallel atmospheric flow in the upper atmosphere, allowing for persistent regeneration of thunderstorms over the same area. These storms formed within an environment that was tropical in nature, connected to a surge of moisture that originated in the Gulf of Mexico. This produced torrential downpours that were capable of producing rain rates of 1-5 inches per hour. Several reports from trusted CoCoRaHS observers across Northeast Minnesota reported accumulations of an inch in 15 to 30 minutes. A widespread area of 3 inches or more accumulated by the morning of Wednesday, June 19 - the majority of which had fallen in eight hours or less. Fifteen COOP or CoCoRaHS observers in Northeast Minnesota reported 5 inches or more, with the highest reports over 7 inches. MRMS estimates suggest that a small area of 8 inches or more may have been possible, in an area not verified with official reports. These reports of 5-7.5+ inches were 500 to 1000+ year rainfalls, with only a 0.1-0.2% chance of happening in any given year. Elsewhere, rainfall over 3 inches in a 6-12 hour period were 100-200 year rainfalls (0.5-1% chance in any given year). Full list of rainfall reports here, or below. The area had been primed for a big flash flooding event, thanks to a wet spring (top 10 wettest March-April-May on record in the Northland), and several moderate to heavy rain events earlier in the month of June.||The impacts of this heavy rain were immediate. During flash flooding on the evening of the 18th, roads across the Iron Range, Lake Vermilion area, Twin Ports, MN North Shore, and WI South Shore were quickly covered with standing and running water, closing and washing out Superior National Forest roads (including access roads to the Boundary Waters Canoe Wilderness, which would strand campers), County Highways (primarily across Cass, Itasca, St. Louis, Lake, Cook, and Bayfield Counties), state highways (notably MN Highways 61, 73, and 1 and WI Highway 13), and U.S. highways (including Highway 53 and 169 and Interstate 35). Homes along the Iron Range and near Lake Vermilion were surrounded by water and some washouts led to homes and businesses being cut off entirely. Numerous cars became stranded after driving into floodwaters. Debris washed onto roads, which made for treacherous nighttime driving conditions in combination with floodwaters. Culvert washouts led to crumbling roads under unsuspecting drivers. Severe thunderstorms occurring at the same time led to pockets of wind damage, one of which caused a tree to fall on a tent, injuring a nine year old boy and triggering a search and rescue operation in Cook County. The I-35 tunnels in Duluth filled with several feet of water through the evening and traffic was rerouted off the interstate. ||The next day, widespread overland flooding began to route into creeks, rivers, and lakes on top of the water that had already immediately fallen into area waterways, continuing extreme rises. Some rivers across the headwaters of the Rainy, Littlefork, Cloquet, and St. Louis rivers rose anywhere from 4 to 20 feet, causing rivers to quickly jump out of banks and lead to another period of minor to major flooding. Area inland lakes saw rises of 1 to 7 feet, especially along the Embarrass River chain of lakes near Biwabik, MN, where drinking water was partially affected. Major flooding occurred along the Littlefork River in the city of Cook, where floodwaters inundated downtown, surrounding residences and businesses with several feet of water for several days. Continued erosion from out-of-bank rivers and creeks continued to work away at area roads and highways, prompting additional road closures. High inflow from the Cloquet River led to water level rises on Island Lake Reservoir and subsequent rapid increase in outflow from the Island Lake Dam (up to 7387 cfs, greater than outflow released during historic flooding of June 2012). This led to extensive flooding downstream of the dam on the Cloquet River which inundated area roads and cut off driveways, encroached on railroad tracks, and surrounded private residences on Hunter and Bowman Lakes. Additional rises on the Mississippi River near Aitkin would briefly hit minor flood stage. Slow moving high water in the Rainy River basin eventually led to minor flooding on Crane, Namakan, and Kabetogama Lakes, thanks to an extra burst of heavy rain early in July.||Damage estimates from the event included $10.5 million in St. Louis County, $1.1 million in Itasca and Lake counties, $400 thousand in Aitkin County, and $205 thousand in Cass County. State and Federal disaster declarations were made for the hardest hit areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Streets and yards in the city of Cook were under water. Low spots of Highway 24 were under water with up to 6 to 12 inches of water across roads. This was following the heavy rainfall on the 18th where 3 to 7 inches of rainfall fell across the region. This led to major flooding occurring along the Littlefork River in the city of Cook, where floodwaters inundated downtown, surrounding residences and businesses with several feet of water, closing dozens of roads, and prompting sandbagging efforts and evacuation of parts of the city. Federal and state disasters were declared once the water receded nearly a week later.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing Storm Recovery Assistance in Beltrami County after severe storms and hurricane-force winds
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A ridge rider pattern continued across the region, with a volatile but slightly capped environment in place heading into the evening of June 28. Remnant boundaries from convection the prior morning provided focus for the new storm development, which had up to 3000 J/kg MUCAPE and around 30 knots of effective shear. Storms remained fairly restrained in the Missouri River Valley fighting the warmest air aloft and weakest shear profiles. Storms coming from northeast South Dakota became the most organized, with a small bowing segment producing damaging winds up to around 65 mph. Other late night storms strengthened moving from far southeast South Dakota across northwest Iowa with wind gusts up to 80 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts measured by the Minnesota RWIS station at Taunton.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing National Guard Assistance in Response to a Severe Winter Storm

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing National Guard Assistance in Response to a Severe Winter Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impactful winter storm brought strong winds and snow to portions of southeast Minnesota throughout the afternoon and evening hours on December 28th. Snowfall totals across southeast Minnesota ranged from 2 to 7 inches with the highest amounts being north of Interstate 90. In addition, the combination of wind gusts of 35 to 55 mph resulted in visibilities dropping to a quarter of a mile or less at times resulting in blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of falling snow and wind gusts of around 40 to 55 mph resulted in very low visibilities during the afternoon and evening hours on December 28th in portions of Olmsted County. Totals snow accumulations across the county ranged from 5 to 7 inches with the highest reported snowfall amount being 6.5 inches 3 miles north-northwest of Rochester.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing National Guard Assistance in Response to a Severe Winter Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent winter storm moved from Kansas northeastward to the Great Lakes on December 28 into the morning hours of December 29. The system brought a leading and more prominent band of snowfall during the morning and midday on December 28, followed by a break in precipitation. As the system deepened during the evening, the band of snowfall wrapped back southward through far eastern South Dakota, southwest Minnesota, and northwest Iowa. When the current and previous snow combined with winds gusting from 40 to 60 mph, widespread blizzard conditions developed from southwest Minnesota into northwest Iowa. State Departments of Transportation advised no travel across southern Minnesota and portions of Iowa from late morning on the 28th through mid-morning of the 29th. Numerous roadways were closed due to numerous crashes. Total snowfall reached as high as 2 to 5 inches in much of southwest Minnesota into northwest Iowa, with 1 to 2 inches along the Missouri River and Interstate 29 corridors and lesser amounts toward the mid James River valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two episodes of extended blizzard conditions occurred over a slightly less than 24 hour period, with a slight improvement in conditions during the mid-afternoon to early evening. Gusty northwest winds from 35 to 50 mph were concurrent with light to moderate snowfall, which totaled 1.5 inches at Edgerton and 1.4 inches at Pipestone. With frequent whiteout conditions reported, travel was not advised.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing National Guard Assistance in Response to a Severe Winter Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter system pivoted over Minnesota and Wisconsin on December 28th, allowing widespread snow to last nearly 24 hours. Surface temperatures started near or slightly above freezing on the morning of the 28th, resulting in a few hours of rain before a rapid cool down occurred and rain transitioned to all snow. As this transition happened, some areas experienced a flash freeze and winds increased out of the northwest, gusting to around 35 to 50 mph. Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. In northwest Iowa, the storm began with several hours of freezing rain, resulting in ice accumulations of one-tenth to one-third of an inch. Additionally, plummeting temperatures created hazardous wind chills ranging from 15 below to 30 below zero.||Transportation was severely disrupted, leading to the closure of the Sioux Falls Regional Airport and most state and federal highways north of Interstate 90; travel was discouraged in nearly all other areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Minnesota Road Weather Information System site near Mountain Lake had frequent sustained winds from 40 to 45 mph with gusts as high as 60 mph.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing National Guard Assistance in Response to a Severe Winter Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale spring storm brought a round of heavy snow to the Upper Mississippi Valley from Saturday, March 14th through Sunday, March 15th. The footprint of the greatest totals stretched from southeast MN into central WI, where many places saw at least a foot of snowfall. The heavy snow combined with strong northwesterly winds resulted in reduced visibilities, often at one mile or less in the heaviest hit areas. Persistent blizzard conditions were most widespread in southern Minnesota, severely deteriorating road conditions. This led to a widespread travel advisory issued by MNDOT for much of the southern portion of the state, including the closure of the southbound lanes of I-35 near Albert Lea.||The highest snowfall reports were:|19.0 inches in Zumbrota, MN (Goodhue).|16.9 inches in Rosemount, MN (Dakota).|16.0 inches in Pine Island, MN (Goodhue).|14.8 inches in Elko New Market, MN (Scott).|14.5 inches in Lakeville, MN (Dakota).|14.5 inches in Prior Lake, MN (Scott).|14.0 inches in western Bloomington, MN (Hennepin).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibilities were dramatically reduced, at or below 1/4 mile for several hours, as heavy snow fell and sustained winds were 15 to 25 mph with frequent gusts over 35 mph. The 2-day snowfall reports ranged from about 10 to 15 inches throughout the county, with the highest report being 16.9 inches in Rosemount. Road conditions became dangerous and the DOT issued a travel advisory on Sunday for the southern portion of the county due to the blizzard conditions.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing National Guard Assistance in Response to a Severe Winter Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A compact low pressure system moved through the region during the early morning hours on March 13th. event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing National Guard Assistance in Response to a Severe Winter Storm

The footprint of the greatest totals stretched from southeast MN into central WI, where many places saw at least a foot of snowfall. The heavy snow combined with strong northwesterly winds resulted in reduced visibilities, often at one mile or less in the heaviest hit areas. Persistent blizzard conditions were most widespread in southern Minnesota, severely deteriorating road conditions. This led to a widespread travel advisory issued by MNDOT for much of the southern portion of the state, including the closure of the southbound lanes of I-35 near Albert Lea.||The highest snowfall reports were:|19.0 inches in Zumbrota, MN (Goodhue).|16.9 inches in Rosemount, MN (Dakota).|16.0 inches in Pine Island, MN (Goodhue).|14.8 inches in Elko New Market, MN (Scott).|14.5 inches in Lakeville, MN (Dakota).|14.5 inches in Prior Lake, MN (Scott).|14.0 inches in western Bloomington, MN (Hennepin).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibilities were dramatically reduced, at or below 1/4 mile for several hours, as heavy snow fell and sustained winds were 15 to 25 mph with frequent gusts over 35 mph. The 2-day snowfall reports ranged from about 8 to 12 inches throughout the county, with the highest report being 12 inches in New Prague. The DOT issued a travel advisory on Sunday due to the blizzard conditions.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing National Guard Assistance in Response to a Severe Winter Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful, but rather moisture starved low pressure system moved across the Northern Plains March 12-13. Widespread high winds raced across the region late on the 12th and into the early overnight of the 13th with gusts ranging from 58 to 78 mph behind a strong cold front. With little to no snow on the ground, there were no significant reductions in visibility.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds were between 40 and 51 mph at times, with gusts as high as 67 mph at a Minnesota Department of Transportation site near Hendricks.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Providing National Guard Assistance in Response to a Severe Winter Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From March 15 through the early hours of March 16, a low-pressure system rapidly intensified over the Central Plains, generating a powerful wind field with gusts reaching 45 to 65 mph. Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. In northwest Iowa, the storm began with several hours of freezing rain, resulting in ice accumulations of one-tenth to one-third of an inch. Additionally, plummeting temperatures created hazardous wind chills ranging from 15 below to 30 below zero.||Transportation was severely disrupted, leading to the closure of the Sioux Falls Regional Airport and most state and federal highways north of Interstate 90; travel was discouraged in nearly all other areas.

During and after a period of heavy snowfall which totaled 6.0 inches 8 miles southeast of Hendricks, visibility was reduced to near zero at times with blowing snow.  U.S. Highway 14 was closed for a time, with travel not recommended over most roadways during the height of the blizzard.

Overall, snowfall totals of over a foot were noted in Winona, Olmsted, Dodge and Wabasha counties with even amounts over 18 inches in Wabasha County. One vehicle accident occurred in Winona County after the snow departed on March 16th resulting in 3 non-life threatening injuries.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This winter storm brought snowfall totals of 4 to 7 inches across Mower County. The highest reported snowfall total was 2 miles southeast of Waltham where 7 inches was measured.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Continuing Assistance to Communities Impacted by Wildfires
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April ended with well above normal precipitation but that quickly transitioned to very dry conditions in May with rainfall amounts only around 5-20% of normal over the first half of the month. Some locations in the Brainerd Lakes area to near Grand Rapids received little, if any precipitation during this time. With green up yet to occur, fuels quickly dried out across the region. May 15th saw a deep low pressure system pass by well to the north setting up westerly to southwesterly winds gusting to 30 to 40 mph the 15th and 16th with very dry conditions lead to Red Flag Warnings across the Northland. Multiple fires began over those two days with two fires, the Flanders Fire and the Stewart Trail Fire becoming quite large and leading to evacuations. The fires spread quickly in those conditions and outside resources were called in to fight the fires. The Flanders Fire reached 1,685 acres in size and was contained on the afternoon of the 20th. The Stewart Trail fire near Two Harbors reached 375 acres in size and destroyed over 30 structures, including homes and cabins along Lake Superior.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Flanders Fire began on Saturday, May 16, 2026, at approximately 12:45PM local time on the northern shore of Flanders Lake near Mission, Minnesota. Very dry and windy conditions were in place with westerly winds gusting to 30 to 40 mph during the early afternoon with relative humidity values falling below 30%, creating dangerous fire weather conditions across the region. The fire was likely started by a campfire and quickly spread to 600 acres by 5:30PM local time that evening. The fire continued to spread overnight and into Sunday the 17th, reaching a maximum size of 1,685 acres. Cooler weather and lighter winds allowed fire crews to make significant progress on the fire reaching 60% containment by late on the 18th and full containment by early evening on the 20th. The fire did not destroy any homes, but a few did sustain damage. A few secondary buildings were destroyed, such as sheds. County Road 11 was closed for a time during the fire and large areas were evacuated ahead of the fire.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report and video received via social media of birch tree downed by gusty non thunderstorm winds. Time estimated based on time post was made to social media, along with maximum gust timing on KROX AWOS and NDAWN station 213629 Greenbush MN, where peak gusts to 45 mph were reported.

event_description: Declaring a Peacetime Emergency and Continuing Assistance to Communities Impacted by Wildfires
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April ended with well above normal precipitation but that quickly transitioned to very dry conditions in May with rainfall amounts only around 5-20% of normal over the first half of the month. Some locations in the Brainerd Lakes area to near Grand Rapids received little, if any precipitation during this time. With green up yet to occur, fuels quickly dried out across the region. May 15th saw a deep low pressure system pass by well to the north setting up westerly to southwesterly winds gusting to 30 to 40 mph the 15th and 16th with very dry conditions lead to Red Flag Warnings across the Northland. Multiple fires began over those two days with two fires, the Flanders Fire and the Stewart Trail Fire becoming quite large and leading to evacuations. The fires spread quickly in those conditions and outside resources were called in to fight the fires. The Flanders Fire reached 1,685 acres in size and was contained on the afternoon of the 20th. The Stewart Trail fire near Two Harbors reached 375 acres in size and destroyed over 30 structures, including homes and cabins along Lake Superior.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Stewart Trail Fire began on Friday, May 15th around 2PM local time near Stewart Trail off County Highway 3 just north of Minnesota Highway 61 in Two Harbors. Very dry and windy conditions were in place with westerly winds gusting to 30 to 40 mph during the early afternoon with relative humidity values falling below 30%, creating dangerous fire weather conditions across the region. The fire was started by a downed power line from the winds and quickly spread to Highway 61 and then up the North Shore to near Castle Danger. Within an hour of the fire starting, structures were being impacted along Highway 61 and the fire was torching in the trees with flames 50 to 60 feet in length in addition to spotting. Highway 61 was quickly closed and evacuations began. Favorable weather conditions, including cooler temperatures, higher humidity, and rainfall, aided firefighters over the weekend allowing the fire to be contained by late afternoon on Monday the 18th. Over 30 structures, including homes and cabins, were destroyed by the fire. The fire reached a maximum size of 375 acres.
